title: Error paths and resource cleanup
goal: After a partial failure, close each stream according to its own state and report the first error.

prerequisites.text: Check fopen before using a FILE * and check fclose afterwards.
Recall the single-owner and single-release rules from the memory module.

terms.title: Open resource
terms.definition: A stream acquired by a successful fopen. The program owes it a fclose call even if another step fails.

terms.title: Primary error
terms.definition: The first error in execution order. In this exercise a later close error does not overwrite it.

terms.title: Controlled failure
terms.definition: A teaching branch that reports a selected failure before calling the operation. It exercises cleanup without harming a file system.

sections.title: Each open stream has its own cleanup check
paragraphs: An operator opens a file for transfer to intake. If the destination cannot open, copying never starts, but the input stream already exists. Input cleanup depends on the input's own state.
Input and output have separate pointers. NULL means that particular stream is absent. Finish in one cleanup block where every acquired stream gets exactly one fclose call.

Record the reason first, then close the streams. Check fclose but use a close error as the status only if there was no earlier error. The counters count fclose calls, including a call that reports an error.

Keep two open flags and one line for the first failure. Both streams open on the normal path. After opening the output fails, the input is still marked open. Check closing each marked stream separately from choosing the final message.

sections.title: The intake file is unavailable, but the log still closes
paragraphs: The fixture input/reading.txt contains 42 and LF. Enter 1 followed by LF in stdin. In this mode a teaching branch skips opening the destination. Input fopen is still real.
In this lab, mode 2 injects a controlled failure before the first actual write. It exercises the cleanup path under the same conditions on every run.
steps: The source stream opens. The output pointer stays NULL.
The primary error becomes open-output-error. Copying does not start.
Cleanup calls fclose for the input and skips the output. Exit code 1 indicates failure.

sections.title: Use the counters to diagnose the cleanup condition
paragraphs: If open-output-error is followed by closed-input 0, check whether input cleanup requires an output stream. In this branch the input opened independently and must be closed.
A too few arguments diagnostic for fclose indicates a missing FILE *. Pass the pointer to an open stream. Never substitute NULL or retry close with the same pointer.

sections.title: Trace a write failure through resource states
paragraphs: In mode 2 both streams open. The program reports write-error before the first write and closes both streams. An empty file may already exist in the run area. Check that a failed run does not offer it as a completed result.

reading.author: ISO/IEC JTC1/SC22/WG14
reading.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 — Programming languages — C
reading.purpose: Review the library contracts used by this stream and its checks.

selfcheck.prompt: Input opened and output did not. Which calls should still happen?
feedback: There is no open output stream.
The successfully opened input still needs its release.
Output failure does not release input.

selfcheck.prompt: Both streams opened and writing was refused. What should the learner see?
options: write-error and one close call for each stream.
feedback: The write step was reached but did not complete.
This run exits with code 1, so it has no successful file result.

selfcheck.prompt: The program first gets write-error, then output fclose returns EOF. Which cause should it print, and why?
selfcheck.feedback: Print write-error because it occurred first. Cleanup still calls fclose. When there is no earlier error, a close failure becomes the reported cause.

practice.title: Copy labels for the next shift
practice.task: The fixture input/labels.txt contains label codes. Stdin selects the mode: empty or 0 means a normal copy, 1 skips output fopen, and 2 refuses the first write for nonempty input. For nonempty stdin use one digit with an optional LF. Only acquired streams are closed. Correct the input cleanup condition. Print the first failure or ok, then the number of fclose calls for each stream. Failure exits with code 1. Success exits with code 0 and an exact labels-copy.txt.

steps.action: Run the starter with 1 in stdin. Find the condition near TODO.
steps.why: The lesson branch skips opening the output. The starter incorrectly ties input cleanup to output.

steps.action: Keep only the input check in the input cleanup condition. Run 1, 2, and 0 separately.
steps.why: Mode 1 never opens the output. In mode 2 both streams opened before failure. Mode 0 completes the copy.
steps.expected: Input/output close calls by mode: 1/0, 1/1, and 1/1. The result file is offered only on success.

criteria: Mode 1 yields open-output-error, closed-input 1, closed-output 0. The output file was never created.
Mode 2 yields write-error with both counters at 1. The failed run does not offer an output to save.
Mode 0 stdout begins with ok and labels-copy.txt contains A7, LF, B4, LF.
practice.hint: After running mode 1, record which stream is already open. Check that the input cleanup decision uses that fact. The counter records calls, so the final status alone is insufficient.

exercises.title: The source never opens
exercises.task: In a separate copy change only the input path to input/missing-labels.txt. Keep mode 0. Predict both counter lines and check whether a result file appears.
criteria: open-input-error, then closed-input 0 and closed-output 0. Code 1. No new file.

teaching.scene: A receiver copies sensor labels. Opening the destination failed, but the source is already open. Decide what still needs closing, then verify the decision with both counters.

predict.prompt: In the example input/reading.txt exists and stdin is 1. Which operation is skipped, and what will the two close counters show?
predict.answer: Mode 1 skips opening received.txt. The input stream was acquired, and the output remains NULL. The result is open-output-error, closed-input 1, closed-output 0, and exit code 1.

apply.prompt: In a separate copy of the example, compare two runs in mode 2. First put a single LF in input/reading.txt, then try an existing empty file. Predict the reason, the two close counts, and the contents of received.txt.
apply.answer: With LF, the loop reads one byte and simulates a failure before writing it. The result is write-error and exit code 1. The empty input immediately reaches EOF with no read error, so the result is ok and exit code 0. Both streams close once in each run, and received.txt is empty in both.

practice.strategy: For each mode, record two separate facts: whether input was acquired and whether output was acquired. Translate them into the expected counters. Preserve the first cause of failure independently.
practice.diagnosis: In mode 1, closed-input 0 with an existing source exposes a cleanup guard error. Opening the output is irrelevant to whether an already open input must be closed.

syntax.explanation: The pointer check protects each stream independently. Incrementing the counter records a call to fclose. The problem == NULL condition preserves the primary error.
syntax.mistake: Do not use the output stream state to guard closing the input. Once a close has been attempted, do not reuse the old pointer.
